title: Sindbad the Seaman and Sindbad the Landsman

full_text:
In the glorious city of Baghdad, in the days of Harun al-Rashid, lived an impoverished porter named Hindbad, who carried heavy crates through the sweltering streets to earn a few coppers for his hungry family.

One suffocating afternoon, exhausted and drenched with sweat, Hindbad set down his load before the bronze gates of a magnificent palace. Cool rosewater breezes drifted from the gardens, accompanied by the melodious plucking of lutes and the savory aroma of roasting meats.

Hindbad sat upon his crate and sighed bitterly: 'How unequal is destiny! Here am I, laboring from dawn to dusk in the burning sun, while the master of this palace lives in paradise, never knowing toil or hunger!'

Suddenly, the portal opened, and a servant summoned Hindbad inside.

The poor porter was ushered into a hall of imperial splendor, paved with marble and lined with silk tapestries. At the head of a banquet table sat a venerable, white-bearded nobleman with eyes full of gentle wisdom. It was Sindbad the Sailor!

Sindbad seated the porter beside him, heaped his plate with roasted meats and almond pastries, and said with tender compassion: 'I overheard your lamentation at my gate, brother. You think that this palace and these treasures fell into my lap without labor. Know, O Hindbad, that every dinar in my coffer was purchased through trials so terrible that my hair turned white in youth! Listen to the history of my seven voyages across the stormy seas, that you may understand that true fortune is forged in the furnace of adversity.'

Hindbad listened with awe, and thus began the famous chronicle of the seven voyages.
moral: Do not envy the wealth of another, for great abundance is often purchased through trials of fire and tears.
